questions.q: Which incident would you most hate to find out about from someone outside?
questions.why: Anchors the log sources that matter.
questions.need: The incident nobody wants to hear about from outside is covered
questions.how: Map the sources and detections that would catch it
questions.listen: A named incident (a leak, a ransom note, a regulator's letter) gives the detections their priority.
questions.probe: Which logs would show that incident starting, and are they collected today?

questions.q: How long did the last real investigation take, from alert to answer?
questions.why: Investigation time is what the platform must cut.
questions.how: Time one investigation and remove the slowest step
questions.listen: Days or weeks means missing logs or manual searching; hours means the basics are in place.
questions.probe: Where did the time go: finding the logs, reading them, or deciding what to do?

questions.q: Which environments send no logs at all today?
questions.why: Blind spots are the first gap to close.
questions.listen: A short, known list is fine; "we are not sure" means blind spots nobody has counted.
questions.probe: Which of those environments would an attacker go to first?

questions.q: Do you know which log sources are expected for each environment, and which are missing?
questions.why: A list of expected sources makes silence visible.
questions.need: Expected log sources are listed, and missing ones are visible
questions.how: Write the expected list per environment
questions.listen: A list per environment, and an alert when a source goes quiet; otherwise silence looks like safety.
questions.probe: When a source stopped sending last time, how long until someone noticed?

questions.q: How many detections are switched on, and how many have fired in the last month?
questions.why: Rules that never fire may be broken, not quiet.
questions.need: Detections that are on actually fire when they should
questions.how: Test the top detections with safe simulations
questions.listen: Many detections on and few firing means noise or broken rules; ask which ones they trust.
questions.probe: Which detection caught something real last month, and which ones nobody believes?

questions.q: Are response playbooks automated for the most common alerts?
questions.why: Automation decides how much the team can handle.
questions.need: Common alerts are handled by automated playbooks
questions.how: Automate the three most frequent responses
questions.listen: Automated containment for the common alerts frees analysts for the ones that need judgement.
questions.probe: Which alert takes most analyst hours, and what do they do every time it fires?

questions.q: How long are logs kept, and is that enough for an investigation or an auditor?
questions.why: Retention gaps appear at the worst moment.
questions.need: Logs are kept long enough for an investigation and an audit
questions.how: Agree retention with legal and the auditors
questions.listen: Kept as long as an investigation looks back, and as long as the auditor asks; cheaper storage for the rest.
questions.probe: How far back did the last investigation, or the last audit, need to look?

questions.q: How many alerts are closed without anyone looking, and who decides that?
questions.need: No alert is closed without someone deciding
questions.how: Make closure need a reason and an owner
questions.listen: Closing alerts unread is a decision; it needs an owner and a rule, not habit.
questions.probe: Who decided which alerts can be closed without a look, and when was that last checked?

questions.q: Who covers the alerts outside working hours, and how fast do they act?
questions.why: Most attacks run at night and at weekends.
questions.need: An alert outside working hours is acted on within an agreed time
questions.how: Name who covers the nights, in house or a service, and the time they act within
questions.listen: A named team or service with a time to act; "the on-call checks in the morning" means hours of free run.
questions.probe: When did the last alert at night get acted on, and by whom?

questions.q: How do you check that a detection still works after a system or a log format changes?
questions.why: Detections break quietly when what they read changes.
questions.need: Detections are tested after changes, and a broken one is noticed
questions.how: Replay a known attack step regularly and check the detection still fires
questions.listen: Tested on a schedule is rare and strong; "we would notice" usually means a broken rule goes unseen for months.
questions.probe: Which detection would you most hate to find broken, and when was it last tested?

questions.q: Which threat intelligence do you use, and who turns it into detections?
questions.why: Intelligence that is never turned into detections is a subscription, not a defence.
questions.need: Threat intelligence that matters to the business becomes detections
questions.how: Pick the sources that fit the business and give someone the job of using them
questions.listen: A person who turns it into detections; a feed straight into the console is noise.
questions.probe: What did the last piece of intelligence change in your detections?

questions.q: After an incident, who must be told, by when, and what must you show them?
questions.why: Reporting duties fix how fast evidence has to be found.
questions.need: What must be reported after an incident, and by when, is known and can be met
questions.how: List the duties to report and the evidence each asks for
questions.listen: A regulator or a customer contract with hours to report makes fast investigation a must.
questions.probe: Could you produce that evidence in time today, and who would gather it?
